Alex Rodriguez was one of baseball's most talented shortstops and third basemen, joining the Yankees in two thousand four and anchoring their offense for twelve seasons. His six hundred ninety-six career home runs, which rank fourth all-time and are just thirty-five short of Barry Bonds' all-time record, his prolific postseason performances, and clutch hitting in the Jeter era made him a key figure in the Yankees' continued relevance, though his legacy was complicated by performance-enhancing drug allegations.

Rodriguez drove in two thousand eighty-six runs, which rank among the all-time greats. He won the American League MVP award in two thousand seven with the Yankees, batting three fourteen with fifty-four home runs and one hundred fifty-six RBIs. A fourteen-time All-Star, Rodriguez won the two thousand nine World Series with the Yankees, his only championship. He hit two ninety-five in postseason play with six home runs in the two thousand nine World Series championship run. In two thousand thirteen, Rodriguez admitted to using performance-enhancing drugs from two thousand one to two thousand three and faced a one hundred sixty-two-game suspension, later reduced, damaging his reputation. He finished his career with the Yankees in two thousand sixteen, providing veteran leadership during a rebuilding period. Derek Jeter was his shortstop and captain, and the two formed the Yankees' power-hitting core. Mariano Rivera, the closer, protected Rodriguez's at-bats in crucial moments. Aaron Judge, a later-era Yankees outfielder, would become the franchise's next superstar. Rodriguez joined the Yankees to pursue a championship with a franchise known for its winning tradition.
